name: Neo-Confederates
summary: Neo-Confederates defend the Confederate cause and the legality of secession, hold that the South is a distinct Christian civilization, and favor states' rights, limited government and free-market economics. The movement arose in reaction to desegregation and is described by historians as continuing the Lost Cause narrative; its most political wing, the League of the South, seeks an independent Southern republic with Anglo-Celtic cultural dominance, while heritage groups such as the Sons of Confederate Veterans emphasize memory and vindication.
scope: The modern neo-Confederate movement as its defining sources describe it: groups and individuals who portray the Confederacy and its cause favourably and defend secession, centred on the League of the South (founded 1994, later the Southern Nationalist League) and on writers and think-tank circles (the Abbeville Institute, the Mises Institute scholars Thomas DiLorenzo, Thomas Woods and Donald Livingston) that SPLC and Political Research Associates tie to it. The sources (SPLC, Hague and Sebesta, Political Research Associates) describe a reactionary, revisionist, white-nationalist branch with Southern nationalism, secession and nullification, Christian nationalism, and free-market or anti-federal economics; heritage groups such as the SCV and UDC are named as part of the movement but disclaim its racial aims. Excludes the historical Confederacy itself, the broader Lost Cause tradition as its own subject, and Southern Democratic politics generally.

notes: Wings differ: heritage groups (SCV, UDC) stress memory and deny racial aims; the League of the South openly advocates white, Anglo-Celtic and Christian dominance. A minority are distributist or claim the Confederacy was socialist. Later pass (2026-11-25): answers rest only on stated positions in SPLC (ideology, League of the South and Michael Hill pages), Political Research Associates, Sebesta and Hague, and key figures' own texts (DiLorenzo's Organized Crime and Mises article, Hill's quoted essays); the earlier Wikipedia-sourced and inferred answers were nulled with reviewHistory. Themes searched: secession, nullification, federalism, immigration, guns and militias, race, segregation and intermarriage, religion and theocracy, sexuality and family, tariffs and free trade, price controls, healthcare, regulation, property, central banking, unions, taxation, drug policy, minimum wage, Lincoln and the war's cause. Woods's How the Catholic Church Built Western Civilization was searched (secession, nullification, Confederate, abortion, usury: no hits; just price, private property, charity: scholastic history, not a position of the movement) and cites nothing. Race, theocracy and antisemitism answers reflect the League wing only partly and are medium confidence where the sources say so.
